extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of Norse mythology, comparative religion, and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading / interpretive essay material about Norse (Scandinavian) mythology, its themes, origins, and character; useful for literary or comparative-religion study. The text discusses cosmology, major figures (Odin, Thor, Balder), motifs (Igdrasil), and cultural values (valor, sincerity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonation of the visible workings of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary characteristic of this old Northland Mythology I find to be Impersonation of the visible workings of Nature: earnest simple recognition of the workings of Physical Nature, as a thing wholly miraculous, stupendous and divine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and elaboration in the text: hostile powers of Nature are Jotuns (Frost, Fire, Sea-tempest); friendly powers (Summer-heat, Sun) are Gods. Specific personifications: Loke as Fire, Thrym/Rime as Frost, Hymir's Cows as Icebergs, Aegir as Sea-tempest, Thor as Thunder. The universe is divided between these personal agencies (Asgard vs Jotunheim). Use such personifications to read Norse mythic imagery as embodiments of natural phenomena rather than abstract allegory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity as the chief poetic and religious quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity is the great characteristic of it. Superior sincerity (far superior) consoles us for the total want of old Grecian grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Norse myth by its 'robust simplicity', homeliness, and directness of conception rather than by classical ideals of grace or theatrical sublimity. The Norse are praised for earnestness, open-eyed wonder, and honest pity (e.g., traits around Thor and Balder). When comparing mythic traditions, prioritize perceived sincerity and earnestness in expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valor as the fundamental moral duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the main practical beliefs: of the Valkyrs and the Hall of Odin; of an inflexible Destiny; and that the one thing needful for a man was to be brave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moral kernel of Norse belief centers on valor: the Valkyrs choose the slain and lead the brave to Odin's hall. Inexorable destiny makes bravery the indispensable ethic. Textual evidence: rituals favoring death in battle, funerary ship-burning, and the cultural shame attached to dying of natural causes. Use these themes to interpret heroism, ethics, and funerary practices in Norse sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Odin as archetypal Thinker/Hero and cultural progenitor
rubrics_metrics.description: Odin is presented as the origin of Norse Mythology: a Teacher, Captain of soul and body, Hero, Prophet — the First Norse Thinker whose articulated thought kindled the people's system of belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess Odin both as mythic deity and as the retrospective figure of a founding thinker: credited with runes (letters), poetry, and the propagation of values (valor). The text argues hero-worship of a great man can evolve into divine status; use this framework when interpreting origin-myths, etymologies (Wuotan/Wodan), and the transformation from historical hero to god in Teutonic traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Igdrasil (the Ash-tree of Existence) as central cosmological metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Igdrasil, the Ash-tree of Existence, figures all Life: its roots in Hela/Death, trunk heaven-high, boughs spread over the Universe; Three Nornas water its roots from the Sacred Well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read cosmological structure, history, and human events through the tree metaphor: roots = past/death, boughs = histories/nations, leaves = individual biographies. The metaphor is used to emphasize interconnectedness across time and the 'infinite conjugation of the verb To do.' Use Igdrasil as a key interpretive image for Norse cosmology and its conceptions of time and fate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eddas as layered, non-coherent summations of successive systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The Eddas are not one coherent System of Thought; but properly the summation of several successive systems. The materials stand at all manner of distances and depths — successive generations contributed and elaborated the Scandinavian system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat contradictions, repetitions, and stylistic differences in the Eddas as the product of cumulative historical layering rather than failures of single authorship. Historical attempts to literalize myths (Snorro, Saxo, Torfaeus) reflect later interpretive practices; scholars should account for stratification, later Skaldic accretions, and editorial/antiquarian reorganizations when reconstructing older beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory and poetic delineation are secondary to active faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory and Poetic Delineation cannot be religious Faith; the Faith itself must first be there, then Allegory enough will gather round it, as the fit body round its soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing poetic or mythic material, distinguish between the original living faith/belief and later poetic elaborations. Later Skaldic songs and prophetic fragments may be 'comparatively idle adjuncts' produced after faith became more self-conscious; prioritize underlying practiced belief over subsequent allegorical or literary ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust homely vigor, pity and directness as aesthetic traits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Norse myths are marked by robust simplicity, veracity, directness of conception, and moments of honest pity (e.g., Balder's death and Frigga's attempt to recover him).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Norse narratives for their untheatrical, 'homely' power: unadorned heroic action, vivid physical detail ('knuckles grow white'), and plain expressions of grief and pity. These aesthetic traits distinguish Norse storytelling from more 'graceful' mythic traditions and should inform readings of tone and moral emphasis.
